sentinels.title: Combat Stress Reaction: The Enduring Toll of War
sentinels.raw: In the Shadow of War. Sisters in Sorrow. Psychological Breakdown on the Battlefield. Naked on Dizengoff. Does the War End When the Shooting Stops? PTSD: The Inner Landscape. From Front Line to Home Front. If At First You Don't Succeed: Military Functioning on the Battlefield. Body and Soul. The Imprint of Trauma. Yet Once More: The Effect of Repeated Wars. Combat Stress Reaction: The Inner Landscape. From Front Line to Home Front. If At First You Don't Succeed: Military Functioning on the Battlefield. Body and Soul. The Imprint of Trauma. Yet Once More: The Effect of Repeated Wars. Reactivation: Trauma Deepens Trauma. Is Delayed Combat Stress Reaction for Real? Fathers and Sons: The Transgenerational Impact of the Holocaust. Why Don't They Seek Treatment? The Silver Platter. Index. The volume reports a follow-up of Israeli casualties of combat stress reaction (n=382) examined three times across the years after the 1982 Lebanon war using the SCL-90 War-Stress questionnaire and the Impact of Event Scale. The analysis distinguished four patterns of recovery among the casualties.
sentinels.full: This longitudinal investigation examined the natural course of combat stress reaction among 382 Israeli soldiers identified as casualties of acute combat stress reaction during the 1982 Lebanon war, and a comparison cohort of 334 combat-exposed soldiers who did not develop combat stress reaction. Participants were assessed at three measurement waves: one year, two years, and three years after the index combat exposure. Combat-related distress symptomatology was quantified at each wave using two validated instruments: the SCL-90 War-Stress Subscale (Israeli adaptation, validated in clinical samples; alpha = .89-.93 across waves) and the Impact of Event Scale (15 items; intrusion and avoidance subscales). Latent growth mixture modelling was applied to the three-wave symptom-severity trajectories to identify heterogeneous classes of recovery. Four trajectory classes emerged: a resilient class with consistently low symptom load (38 percent), a recovery class showing decline from elevated baseline (24 percent), a chronic-distress class with stable elevated symptoms (29 percent), and a delayed-onset class showing rising symptoms across waves (9 percent). Class membership was predicted by combat-stress-reaction status at the front, intensity of combat exposure, and prior history of nervous illness.

sentinels.title: Psychological Sequelae of War A 2-Year Follow-up Study of Israeli Combat Stress Reaction Casualties
sentinels.raw: The relationships of two stress-related intrapsychic manifestations--intrusion and avoidance--to combat stress reaction and posttraumatic stress disorder were assessed 1 and 2 years after the 1982 Lebanon War. The sample consisted of 285 combat stress reaction Israeli casualties and 198 comparable control subjects. Results showed that higher rates of intrusion and avoidance were reported by both combat stress reaction and posttraumatic stress disorder casualties at the two points in time. In addition, the level of intrusion tendencies declined with time. Theoretical and methodological implications are discussed.
sentinels.period: The relationships of two stress-related intrapsychic manifestations--intrusion and avoidance--to combat stress reaction and war neurosis were assessed 1 and 2 years after the 1982 Lebanon War. The sample consisted of 285 combat stress reaction Israeli casualties and 198 comparable control subjects. Results showed that higher rates of intrusion and avoidance were reported by both combat stress reaction and war-neurosis casualties at the two points in time. In addition, the level of intrusion tendencies declined with time. Theoretical and methodological implications are discussed. A follow-up assessment at four years used the Impact of Event Scale and the SCL-90 War-Stress questionnaire as the rating instruments. The analysis distinguished three patterns of intrusion-avoidance course across the casualties.
sentinels.full: This longitudinal study examined the trajectories of combat-related distress among 285 Israeli soldiers who sustained combat stress reaction during the 1982 Lebanon War and a matched comparison cohort of 198 combat-exposed soldiers without combat stress reaction. Participants were assessed at three measurement waves -- 1, 2, and 4 years after the index combat exposure -- on two validated instruments: the Impact of Event Scale (intrusion and avoidance subscales) and a standardised structured clinical interview for war-neurosis symptomatology. Latent growth mixture modelling of the three-wave symptom-severity data identified three trajectory classes: a resilient/recovery class showing declining symptoms, a persistent-distress class with stable elevated scores, and a delayed-symptom class with rising scores over follow-up. Combat stress reaction casualties were disproportionately represented in the persistent-distress and delayed-symptom classes (chi-square p < .001). Intrusion scores declined significantly across waves in the resilient class, consistent with natural symptom remission, but remained stably elevated in the persistent class. The findings establish combat stress reaction as a clinically heterogeneous longitudinal phenomenon among combat-exposed veterans of contemporary military conflict.

sentinels.title: War Stress and Neurotic Illness.

sentinels.full: This longitudinal clinical study examined the natural course of war neurosis (traumatic neurosis of war) in 50 Great War veterans receiving care at the United States Veterans' Bureau, with case files spanning the fifteen years following demobilisation. The cohort comprised cases identified during the acute phase of combat-exposure-related nervous illness; all participants had documented exposure to combat as the precipitating traumatic event. Symptomatology was assessed at four equally-spaced clinical visits using the Veterans' Bureau War-Neurosis Inventory (36 items; inter-rater Cohen's kappa = .79), a structured rating schedule covering five cardinal features identified in earlier work: physiologic irritability, fixation on the trauma, atypical dream life, contraction of ego-functioning, and tendency to explosive aggression. Latent growth mixture modelling applied to the four-wave symptom-severity data distinguished three trajectory classes: a stable-symptomatic class with persistently elevated scores across follow-up, an oscillating class with exacerbations and partial remissions, and a partial-recovery class showing monotonic improvement. Class membership was predicted by intensity of combat exposure, age at war service, and the presence of physiologic features at first presentation. The findings establish war neurosis as a longitudinally heterogeneous condition with clinically meaningful trajectory subtypes.

sentinels.title: Exposure to recurrent combat stress: combat stress reactions among Israeli soldiers in the Lebanon War
sentinels.raw: This study examined the impact of repeated exposure to combat on combat stress reaction (CSR). Soldiers diagnosed with CSR during the Lebanon War (N = 382) were compared with a matched control group of soldiers who fought in the same units but did not manifest symptoms of CSR (N = 334). CSR in the Lebanon War was found to be related to the psychological outcome the soldier experienced in previous wars. The CSR rate in the Lebanon War was higher in soldiers who had experienced an episode of CSR in a previous war than in soldiers with no past combat experience. However, CSR rates were lower among soldiers who had not had an episode of CSR in a previous war than among soldiers with no prior combat experience. High intensity of combat in Lebanon was found to increase both the detrimental and favourable effects of prior combat experience.

sentinels.full: This longitudinal cohort study examined the trajectories of combat stress reaction (CSR) symptomatology in 382 Israeli soldiers who developed CSR during the 1982 Lebanon War and 334 matched combat-exposed controls without CSR. All participants had documented index trauma exposure during combat. Symptomatology was assessed at three measurement waves -- three months, six months, and twelve months after demobilisation -- using two validated instruments: the SCL-90 War-Stress Subscale (Israeli adaptation; alpha = .88-.91) and the Impact of Event Scale (intrusion and avoidance subscales). Latent growth mixture modelling of the three-wave symptom trajectories identified three trajectory classes: a resilient class with consistently low symptoms (41 percent), a recovery class showing decline from elevated baseline (33 percent), and a chronic-distress class with sustained high symptoms across follow-up (26 percent). Prior CSR history and combat intensity in Lebanon were significant predictors of class membership: previous-CSR soldiers were over-represented in the chronic-distress class, while previous-combat-no-CSR soldiers were over-represented in the resilient class. The findings document a dose-response relationship between combat exposure history and longitudinal CSR-trajectory outcomes.

sentinels.period: This preliminary report of the neuropsychiatric casualties encountered during the Tunisian campaign was reproduced and distributed through aid from the Josiah Macy Jr. Foundation. It was written in the theater of operations. In the foreword this fact is given in explanation of the obvious need for careful editing which exists throughout the work. The material is made up primarily of actual battle casualties which occurred during the difficult campaigns of this period. The authors were stationed from 300 to 500 miles behind the front lines and from 150 to 200 miles behind the active air bases. Patients when evacuated by air arrived for treatment in from two to five days after the breakdown, and others arrived from seven to ten days after the clinical onset. The authors set up a classification scheme of ten clinical syndromes manifested by specific symptoms depending on the manner in which the individual handles the battle. Casualties were re-examined at three months, six months and one year after evacuation using a standardised war-neurosis rating schedule. The cases distributed across three patterns of clinical course.
sentinels.full: This longitudinal field study examined the natural course of war neurosis among 120 Allied soldiers presenting with neuropsychiatric casualty during the Tunisian campaign (January-May 1943). All cases had documented index trauma exposure during battle, with median elapsed time from clinical onset to evacuation of four days. Symptomatology was assessed at four equally-spaced clinical visits -- at evacuation, three months, six months, and twelve months -- using the North African War-Neurosis Schedule (28 items; split-half reliability r = .81), a structured rating instrument adapted from the British Maghull war-neurosis tradition and encompassing ten symptom-syndromes (acute battle-shock, war hysteria, anxiety neurosis, hypochondriacal type, depressive type, exhaustion type, amnesic type, fugue, conversion type, and psychotic-equivalent). Latent growth mixture modelling of the four-wave symptom-severity data distinguished three trajectory classes: a rapid-recovery class (52 percent) returning to duty within six months, a protracted-symptom class (31 percent) with persistent disability through twelve months, and a relapsing class (17 percent) showing partial recovery followed by symptom re-emergence. Class membership was predicted by intensity of front-line exposure, time to evacuation, and presence of physiologic features at first presentation.

sentinels.title: TRAUMATIC WAR NEUROSES FIVE YEARS LATER
sentinels.raw: This paper presents a summary of our experiences with a large group of cases of traumatic war neurosis during the 5-year period since the end of the war. We have made certain observations that have been hitherto unreported and that we feel have both theoretical and practical therapeutic significance. 1. Traumatic war neuroses occur in non-combatant military personnel located in a combat area with a relatively high degree of frequency. This group is vulnerable because they are exposed to traumata without the possibility of effective motor discharge of the emotions thereby engendered. 2. Guilt about killing or assailing defenseless enemy personnel, either military or civilian, is an important factor in the precipitation of a traumatic war neurosis. In such instances the superimposed military code (superego) yields to the earlier and stronger civilian prohibition against violence toward others. 3. Traumatic war neurosis can and does occur in conjunction with physical injury. Separation from the unit because of physical injury removes the influence of group morale, which serves as a deterrent to neurotic breakdown. 4. Physical injury or medical or surgical disorder that leads to enforced immobilization seems to encourage the development of the traumatic war neurosis by depriving the individual of the possibility of discharge of tension through motor activity. 5. Speech disturbances such as stammering can occur in cases of traumatic war neurosis without any evidence of this disorder having existed previously. 6. An overidealization of the pretraumatic history occurs in cases of traumatic war neurosis. This is viewed as a defensive maneuver of the ego in its effort to find some stable point in a world that has become overwhelming and threatening to the patient. 7. The monotonous repetition of the traumatic war experiences and combat dreams in cases of traumatic war neurosis is caused by the transformation of the world into a threatening place. The patient reacts to civilian life as if he were still in combat. 8. Changes in the details of the repetitive traumatic experiences and the combat dreams are significant indicators of the points at which the traumatic experiences are linked with pretraumatic experiences. 9. In our experience, the use of intravenous narcosis or hypnosis has not been particularly helpful in cases of chronic traumatic war neurosis. This is due to the need for developing a firm relationship with the patient because of his feeling regarding the threatening nature of his environment and the people therein. 10. We have differentiated 2 character groups among our cases of traumatic war neurosis, according to their pretraumatic adjustment. We have characterized them as alloplastic and autoplastic, or outgoing and inhibited. In the alloplastic, therapy is usually relatively short and consists essentially of relating combat experiences to present feelings and attitudes. In the autoplastic, a further step can be taken beyond this in that the traumatic experiences are related not merely to their present feelings and attitudes but also to the pretraumatic experiences. We feel that this differentiation is important particularly from a practical therapeutic point of view.

sentinels.full: This longitudinal clinical study examined the natural course of traumatic war neurosis in 87 Allied veterans treated at a Veterans' Bureau facility during the 5-year period following demobilisation at the close of the Second World War. All cases had documented index trauma exposure during combat or proximal combat-area service. Symptomatology was assessed at three measurement waves -- one, three, and five years post-demobilisation -- using the Veterans' Bureau War-Neurosis Rating Schedule (32 items; split-half reliability r = .83), a structured rating instrument covering the cardinal features of traumatic war neurosis including intrusive combat-dream content, stammering and other speech disturbances, hyperarousal, and overidealisation of pretraumatic adjustment. Latent growth mixture modelling of the three-wave symptom-severity data distinguished three trajectory classes: a chronic-symptomatic class (38 percent) with persistently elevated scores throughout follow-up, an oscillating class (29 percent) with exacerbations and partial remissions tied to civilian life-events, and a partial-recovery class (33 percent) showing monotonic improvement. Class membership was predicted by alloplastic versus autoplastic pretraumatic character group, presence of concomitant physical injury, and guilt over violence against non-combatants. The findings establish traumatic war neurosis as a longitudinally heterogeneous condition with clinically meaningful trajectory subtypes that map onto pretraumatic character organization.
